title: Health outcomes associated with crack-cocaine use: Systematic review and meta-analyses

claims.statement: Crack and powder are the same drug in two forms, and the sources read describe what differs as the route each form allows, the amounts and patterns of use that go with it, and the circumstances of the people using it, rather than a property of crack itself; no source read tests crack against powder with those differences accounted for. Powder cannot be smoked because it breaks down at the temperature needed, while the base form (crack) can, so the form sets the route; once in the blood, a narrative review describes the two forms as eliminated and broken down alike, with smoked and injected cocaine reaching peak blood levels within about 5 minutes against about 30 to 40 minutes for snorting (second-hand from studies not read here; Hatsukami & Fischman, 1996). In US household surveys of 1995–1998, among 855 people who had started cocaine within the previous 0–23 months, each of seven dependence features was reported about 2 to 4 times as often by the 190 who had started crack as by the 572 who had started powder and never used crack (weighted occurrence in the past year about 18% to 32% against about 5% to 12%); the summary odds ratio across features, adjusted for sex, age, race, daily drinking, daily tobacco smoking, injecting and the number of days cocaine was used, was 1.9 (95% CI 1.4 to 2.5), and 1.6 (1.0 to 2.5) for 93 people who had started crack after two or more years of powder use; without the term for days of use the estimate was about 2.3 to 3.7, reported without intervals (Chen & Anthony, 2004). Those estimates come from one interview, with use, form and problems all self-reported and no measure of how people differed before they started; the authors say a greater susceptibility among people who start crack cannot be ruled out, and adjusting for days of use may remove part of a real difference because dependence itself raises use. A 2017 systematic review of 302 studies pooled comparisons of crack use with no crack use, not with powder: comparisons of people who used crack with people who used other forms of cocaine were described as mixed for anxiety disorders, dependence on alcohol, cocaine or other substances, and depression (12 studies), and as showing no difference for 10 other diagnoses (5 studies), and none of them was pooled or tested; the review's own authors state that crack is not a plausible direct cause of the infections and violence it found associated with crack use, which they read as markers of risk behaviours and environments (Butler et al., 2017). The 1996 review, whose evidence is uncontrolled and mostly from the mid-1980s to early 1990s, reports that people who smoke or inject use cocaine more often and in larger amounts than people who snort it and reach regular use, problems and treatment sooner; its support for the statement that differences disappear once the amount used is held constant rests partly on two sets of meeting proceedings published before crack appeared. In the sources read, no comparison of crack with powder adjusts for amount used, other drug use, income, housing or the policing people met. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Chen & Anthony (2004), weighted past-year occurrence of seven dependence features among people who had started cocaine 0–23 months before: about 5% to 12% in the powder-only group; about 18% to 32% in the group who had recently started crack and about 11% to 33% in the group who had started crack after two or more years of powder use (the group ranges are the first reader's readings of a figure that prints no values). Unadjusted odds ratios, recent crack against powder only: reduced activities 5.6 (1.9 to 15.9), tolerance 4.8 (1.8 to 12.6), inability to cut down 4.0 (1.9 to 8.7), emotional problems 3.5 (1.6 to 7.7), salience 3.4 (1.5 to 7.7), using more than intended 3.1 (1.4 to 7.0), health problems 3.0 (0.9 to 9.7). Adjusted summary across the seven features: 1.9 (1.4 to 2.5) for recent crack and 1.6 (1.0 to 2.5) for crack after two or more years of powder; about 2.3 to 3.7 without the days-of-use term (no intervals). These are odds ratios although the paper calls them relative risks; from the figure the corresponding prevalence ratios are about 1.5 to 4.4 (study card's calculation). Butler et al. (2017): no pooled crack-versus-powder estimate; 12 studies mixed and 5 showing no difference, none tested. Hatsukami & Fischman (1996), second-hand: two thirds of people smoking crack used daily against 18% of people snorting powder; in the 1991 national survey, crack use was 52.5% among frequent and 17.5% among infrequent past-year cocaine use, injecting 24.3% against 9.3%.
